citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix $m\ge1$ and angles $0<\theta_j<\pi$ for $1\le j\le m$. On the strip $S=\mathbb R\times[0,1]$ impose the real product-plane boundary conditions $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$ and $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Let $H^1_\theta$ be the completion of smooth maps satisfying these conditions and compactly supported in the $s$ direction, for the norm
$$\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|u_s\|_2^2+\|u_t\|_2^2.$$
The real linear operator $D=\partial_s+i\partial_t$ extends to an isomorphism $H^1_\theta\to L^2(S;\mathbb C^m)$. Put $\gamma=\min_j\{\theta_j,\pi-\theta_j\}>0$. Its inverse satisfies
$$\|D^{-1}f\|_2\le\gamma^{-1}\|f\|_2,\qquad \|D^{-1}f\|_{H^1}\le\sqrt{\gamma^{-2}+5}\,\|f\|_2.$$
For $0\le\delta<\gamma$, set $w(s)=e^{\delta|s|}$, $H^1_{\theta,\delta}=\{u:wu\in H^1_\theta\}$ with norm $\|wu\|_{H^1}$, and $L^2_\delta=\{f:wf\in L^2\}$ with norm $\|wf\|_2$. Then $D:H^1_{\theta,\delta}\to L^2_\delta$ is an isomorphism and
$$\|D^{-1}f\|_{H^1_{\theta,\delta}}\le\frac{\sqrt{\gamma^{-2}+5}}{1-\delta/\gamma}\,\|f\|_{L^2_\delta},\qquad \|wD^{-1}f\|_2\le\frac{\|wf\|_2}{\gamma-\delta}.$$
These are estimates for the constant linear asymptotic model. They make no assertion about nonlinear strip decay, a variable-coefficient operator, or its Maslov index.

Assume Countable Choice. On $S=\mathbb R\times[0,1]$ use the real Hilbert domain $H^1_\theta$ with product-line boundary conditions at angles $0<\theta_j<\pi$: it is the $H^1$ completion of smooth maps compactly supported in the first coordinate and satisfying $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$, $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Let $B(s,t)$ be a bounded measurable real linear endomorphism of $\mathbb C^m$. Suppose there are real diagonal constant matrices $B_\pm=\operatorname{diag}(b_{\pm,1},\ldots,b_{\pm,m})$ such that
$$\underset{\pm s>R,\ 0<t<1}{\operatorname{ess\,sup}}\|B(s,t)-B_\pm\|\longrightarrow0\quad(R\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and $\theta_j-b_{\pm,j}\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ for every $j$ and each sign. Then
$$T=\partial_s+i\partial_t+B(s,t):H^1_\theta\longrightarrow L^2(S;\mathbb C^m)$$
is bounded and Fredholm over $\mathbb R$: its kernel and cokernel are finite dimensional and its range is closed. There are bounded left and right parametrices whose errors are operator-norm limits of finite-rank operators. No index value or identification with a Maslov index is asserted.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb F$
([[def-banach-space]]) and let $T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is a **Fredholm operator** when
all three of the following hold:

1. $\ker T$ is finite dimensional, that is, admits an ordered basis of finite
   length ([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-dimension]]);
2. $\operatorname{ran}T$ is a closed subspace of $Y$
   ([[def-linear-subspace]]);
3. the **cokernel** $\operatorname{coker}T:=Y/\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite
   dimensional ([[def-quotient-vector-space-coset-notation]],
   [[def-dimension]]).

Here the cokernel is the algebraic quotient vector space; it also carries the
quotient seminorm of [[def-quotient-seminorm]], which is a norm when the range
is closed ([[thm-quotient-seminorm-is-a-norm-iff-subspace-is-closed]]), but the dimension in clause 3 is the vector-space dimension of the
quotient and does not depend on that norm.

For a Fredholm operator $T$ the **index** of $T$ is the integer

$$\operatorname{ind}T:=\dim_{\mathbb F}\ker T-\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{coker}T$$

Here subtraction is in $\mathbb Z$, not in $\mathbb N$: write $a=\dim_{\mathbb F}\ker T$ and $b=\dim_{\mathbb F}\operatorname{coker}T$ and identify a natural $n$ with $[(n,0)]$. Precisely,

$$\operatorname{ind}T=[(a,b)]=[(a,0)]+(-[(b,0)])\in\mathbb Z$$

by [[def-integers]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Both dimensions are natural numbers, so this class is defined even when $a<b$; the index may be positive, negative or zero.

**Two remarks on the definition.** The closedness of the range is listed
explicitly as a hypothesis of the definition rather than extracted from the
other clauses. And no property of the index is asserted here; additivity,
local constancy and invariance under compact perturbations are separate
theorems.

derivations.claim: **A local index calculation for perturbations.** Fix any operator $A:X\to Y$ in [F2]. Write $K=\ker A$, $Z=K^\perp$, $R=\operatorname{ran}A$ and $C=R^\perp$. These orthogonal decompositions exist under the choice hypothesis by [F2]; $K,C$ are finite dimensional. The restriction $A_Z:Z\to R$ is bijective: subtracting the kernel projection from a preimage proves surjectivity, and injectivity follows from $Z\cap K=0$. The bound in [F2] makes its inverse bounded, with norm at most $c_A^{-1}$. For a bounded perturbation $E:X\to Y$ of norm less than $c_A$, order the source as $Z\oplus K$ and target as $R\oplus C$. The first block $L=A_Z+E_{RZ}$ is invertible by the norm-convergent Neumann series for $1+A_Z^{-1}E_{RZ}$. The full matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}L&E_{RK}\\E_{CZ}&E_{CK}\end{pmatrix}$. The invertible source change $(z,k)\mapsto(z+L^{-1}E_{RK}k,k)$ and target change $(r,c)\mapsto(r,c-E_{CZ}L^{-1}r)$ reduce it to $\operatorname{diag}(L,F)$, where $F=E_{CK}-E_{CZ}L^{-1}E_{RK}:K\to C$. Its kernel and cokernel are those of this finite-dimensional $F$. Rank-nullity gives $\dim\ker F-\dim(C/\operatorname{ran}F)=\dim K-\dim C$. Thus every sufficiently small bounded perturbation has the same index as $A$, with an explicit finite-dimensional proof.

**The step operator's kernel.** For the diagonal step operator $D+B^0$ from the Statement, [F1] diagonalizes the operator on the real modes. Put $\lambda_- =\pi n-\theta_j+b_{-,j}$ and $\lambda_+=\pi n-\theta_j+b_{+,j}$ for one mode. A weak solution of $a'+\lambda(s)a=0$ equals $c e^{-\lambda_-s}$ on $s<0$ and $c e^{-\lambda_+s}$ on $s>0$. Indeed multiplication by the smooth integrating factor on either half-line leaves a distribution with zero derivative, hence a constant; a distribution annihilating derivatives is constant because every compactly supported smooth test of integral zero is the derivative of another such test. The constants agree at zero, since a jump would contribute a point mass to $a'$ whereas $-\lambda(s)a$ is locally integrable. This solution is in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ precisely when $\lambda_-<0<\lambda_+$, or $c=0$. In the nonzero case its derivative is bounded in absolute value by $\max\{|\lambda_-|,|\lambda_+|\}|a|$, so it is in $H^1$ and gives a vector in $X$. Only finitely many $(j,n)$ can have this sign pattern, as $m$ is finite and $\pi n$ tends to the respective infinities. Orthogonality of the modes gives exactly one independent real generator per such pair, and no other kernel vectors.

**Reduction to a diagonal step operator.** Let $B^0$ be the step function in the Statement and set $B^r=(1-r)B+rB^0$ for $0\le r\le1$. Every $B^r$ has exactly the same diagonal limits and nondegeneracy; hence $T_r=D+B^r$ is Fredholm by [F2]. Also $\|T_r-T_q\|_{X\to Y}\le |r-q|\|B^0-B\|_\infty$, so this is a norm-continuous path. At each parameter, step 1.1 makes its integer index locally constant. A locally constant function on the connected interval $[0,1]$ is constant: the inverse image of one value and its complement would otherwise be two disjoint nonempty open subsets. Consequently $\operatorname{ind}T=\operatorname{ind}(D+B^0)$. No compact-perturbation or general Banach open-mapping theorem is used.

**The step operator's cokernel.** Since its range is closed, the orthogonal projection in [F2] identifies the cokernel with the vectors $g\in Y$ orthogonal to its range. Test this orthogonality on $a(s)e_{j,n}(t)$ with $a$ real, smooth and compactly supported. For the real modal coefficient $g_{j,n}$ it says $\int g_{j,n}(a'+\lambda(s)a)=0$, equivalently $-g'_{j,n}+\lambda(s)g_{j,n}=0$ in distributions. The integrating-factor argument of step 1.2 gives $g_{j,n}(s)=c e^{\lambda_-s}$ on $s<0$ and $c e^{\lambda_+s}$ on $s>0$, with one common constant. It is in $L^2$ precisely when $\lambda_->0>\lambda_+$, or $c=0$. There are finitely many such pairs. Conversely each of these coefficient functions is orthogonal to the image of every smooth finite modal sum, by integration by parts in $s$. Such sums are dense in $X$ by [F1], and the operator is bounded, so it is orthogonal to the whole range. Thus these are exactly the claimed real cokernel generators.

**Counting the signs.** For one $(j,n)$, its contribution to kernel dimension minus cokernel dimension is $\mathbf1_{\lambda_{-,j,n}<0}-\mathbf1_{\lambda_{+,j,n}<0}$. The two indicators agree for all sufficiently large positive or negative $n$. Since neither limiting eigenvalue vanishes, $\lambda_{\pm,j,n}<0$ is exactly $n<(\theta_j-b_{\pm,j})/\pi$, whose threshold is not an integer. Summing the finite difference of these two integer half-lines gives $\lfloor(\theta_j-b_{-,j})/\pi\rfloor-\lfloor(\theta_j-b_{+,j})/\pi\rfloor$. Summing over the finitely many components, and using the preceding kernel, cokernel and continuation calculations and [F3], proves the displayed index formula for the original real-linear $B$ as well as the step model. The calculation allows either index sign and zero index, including the constant case $B_-=B_+$.

**Fixed-end weights.** For $w=e^{\delta|s|}$, the weak product rule gives $wT(w^{-1}v)=Dv+(B-\delta\operatorname{sign}(s))v$. This identity follows by splitting integration by parts into the two half-strips; there is no point mass at zero because $w$ is continuous. Multiplication by $w$ identifies the specified weighted spaces isometrically with $X,Y$, and the new diagonal limits are $b_{-,j}+\delta$ and $b_{+,j}-\delta$. The minimum limiting spectral gap is positive: for each of finitely many nonintegral thresholds its distance to the integer lattice is positive. Under the bound on $\delta$, none of the corresponding limiting modal eigenvalues changes sign. Hence the new operator satisfies [F2] and its two floor terms in step 3.1 are unchanged. The weighted index is therefore the same. These arguments prove the stated fixed-end operator result; no geometric bundle or Maslov identification has entered the proof.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $m\ge1$ and $0<\theta_j<\pi$. Let $X=H^1_\theta$ be the real Hilbert completion, in the norm $(\|u\|_2^2+\|u_s\|_2^2+\|u_t\|_2^2)^{1/2}$, of smooth maps on $\mathbb R_s\times[0,1]_t$ compactly supported in $s$ and satisfying $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m$, $u(s,1)\in\prod_j e^{i\theta_j}\mathbb R$. Put $Y=L^2(\mathbb R\times[0,1];\mathbb C^m)$, regarded as a real Hilbert space. Suppose $B(s,t)$ is an essentially bounded measurable real linear endomorphism and has real diagonal limits $B_\pm=\operatorname{diag}(b_{\pm,j})$ uniformly in essential supremum as $s\to\pm\infty$, with $\theta_j-b_{\pm,j}\notin\pi\mathbb Z$. Then the bounded Fredholm operator
$$T=\partial_s+i\partial_t+B:X\longrightarrow Y$$
has real index
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}T=\sum_{j=1}^m\left(\left\lfloor\frac{\theta_j-b_{-,j}}\pi\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{\theta_j-b_{+,j}}\pi\right\rfloor\right).$$
For the diagonal step function $B^0(s)=B_-$ for $s<0$ and $B_+$ for $s\ge0$, the kernel has one real generator for every $(j,n)\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\mathbb Z$ with $\lambda_{-,j,n}<0<\lambda_{+,j,n}$, and the cokernel has one for every pair with $\lambda_{-,j,n}>0>\lambda_{+,j,n}$, where $\lambda_{\pm,j,n}=\pi n-\theta_j+b_{\pm,j}$.

The same index holds on the two-sided weighted spaces $X_\delta=\{u:e^{\delta|s|}u\in X\}$ and $Y_\delta=\{f:e^{\delta|s|}f\in Y\}$ whenever $0\le\delta<\min_{j,\pm,n}|\lambda_{\pm,j,n}|$. This is an index theorem for this specified strip operator and product-line domain; it does not identify the pullback operator of a general geometric strip or assert a Heegaard-domain Maslov formula.

derivations.claim: **The gauge and its exact domains.** Choose the unique $\theta_0\in(0,\pi)$ representing $\vartheta_-$ modulo $\pi$ and put $a(s)=\vartheta(s)-\theta_0$, $U(s,t)=e^{ia(s)t}$. The functions $a,a'$ are bounded, with $a'$ compactly supported. Multiplication by $U$ is an invertible real linear map of smooth maps compactly supported in $s$. At $t=0$ it is the identity, and at $t=1$ it sends $e^{i\theta_0}\mathbb R$ to $e^{i\vartheta(s)}\mathbb R$. Its two derivatives are $U_s=i a'(s)tU$ and $U_t=i a(s)U$. Therefore the product rule gives a constant $C$ with $\|Uv\|_{H^1}\le C\|v\|_{H^1}$, and the same bound holds for $U^{-1}$ with possibly a different $C$. These maps extend by completion to mutually inverse bounded maps $H^1_{\theta_0}\leftrightarrow X_\vartheta$. They are also unitary on the real $L^2$ target. This proves the precise domain identification, including the variable boundary, without assuming any prior boundary-trivialization theorem.

**Conjugate the operator, retaining both zeroth-order terms.** For a smooth compactly supported $v$ in the fixed-line domain, direct differentiation gives $U^{-1}\mathcal D(Uv)=\partial_s v+i\partial_t v+Bv$, where $B=-a(s)+i a'(s)t+U^{-1}A(s,t)U$. The term $-a$ comes from $iU_t=-aU$, and the term $i a't$ comes from $U_s$; both signs are therefore fixed by the specified Cauchy–Riemann convention. The last term is a real linear endomorphism even if $A$ is not complex linear. It is bounded and tends uniformly to zero, because $U$ is pointwise unitary. Since $a'$ vanishes on the ends, the limits of $B$ are the real scalar constants $b_\pm=-(\vartheta_\pm-\theta_0)$. In particular $\theta_0-b_\pm=\vartheta_\pm\notin\pi\mathbb Z$. The identity extends to the completions by the bounds of step 1.1 and boundedness of each displayed first- and zeroth-order term.

**Index and endpoint normalization.** Apply [F1] to the operator in step 2.1. Its real index is $\lfloor(\theta_0-b_-)/\pi\rfloor-\lfloor(\theta_0-b_+)/\pi\rfloor=\lfloor\vartheta_-/\pi\rfloor-\lfloor\vartheta_+/\pi\rfloor$. The bounded source and target isomorphisms of step 1.1 identify kernels and ranges and induce an isomorphism of cokernels, so this is the index of $\mathcal D$ too. Changing the global lift by one constant integer multiple of $\pi$ adds the same integer to both floor terms and does not alter their difference. If the end lines coincide, their given lift difference is $k\pi$ and the result is exactly $-k$. This agrees with boundary orientation: for $ds\wedge dt$, the outward-normal-first convention gives tangent $+\partial_s$ on $t=0$ and $-\partial_s$ on $t=1$, so a lift increasing by $k\pi$ along increasing $s$ on the upper edge makes $-k$ turns in the unoriented-line circle along its oriented traversal. No translation direction has been removed from the operator's domain or index.

**Weights and the product version.** The gauge $U$ commutes with scalar multiplication by $w=e^{\delta|s|}$, and its bounded derivative estimates in step 1.1 apply to $w v$ as well. Thus it identifies the weighted variable-line domain and target with the weighted fixed-line spaces. The fixed-line limiting eigenvalues are $\pi n-\theta_0+b_\pm=\pi n-\vartheta_\pm$, whose minimum absolute value is exactly the distance stated in the claim. The weighted conclusion follows from [F1]. For finitely many components use $U=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i(\vartheta_j(s)-\theta_{0,j})t})$, with $\theta_{0,j}\in(0,\pi)$ the residue of $\vartheta_{j,-}$. The same differentiation gives real diagonal limits $b_{\pm,j}=-(\vartheta_{j,\pm}-\theta_{0,j})$ even when $A$ mixes the components and their conjugates. Apply the full real-linear version of [F1] and sum its floor differences. This proves every asserted framed strip formula under precisely Countable Choice; no general geometric Maslov identification is presumed.
